Cournot duopoly: Q = 60, P = 60; with n firms Q = 90n/(n + 1), approaching competition as n grows
Bertrand with homogeneous goods: P = MC = 30 with just two firms, so the mode of competition can matter more than numbers
Stackelberg: Q = 67.5, P = 52.5; timing and commitment affect outcomes for given n
Bertrand paradox is fragile: capacity constraints (Kreps and Scheinkman, 1983) can give Cournot-like outcomes; differentiation also softens price competition
Collusion: repeated interaction can sustain monopoly prices; the critical discount factor rises with n, so numbers matter through sustainability
Mode of competition is partly endogenous: capacity, product design and market structure shape whether firms set quantities or prices
Concentration measures (e.g. HHI) linked to Cournot mark-ups; the Lerner index equals share/|ε| in Cournot
Policy implications: merger control, coordinated and unilateral effects
Reasoned conclusion: both matter and interact; the claim is partly true but overstated
questions.modelAnswer:
Using the illustrative market, a monopoly produces 45 at P = 75, while perfect competition produces 90 at P = 30. Cournot duopolists each produce 30, so Q = 60 and P = 60. With n Cournot firms, total output is 90n/(n + 1): 67.5 with three firms, about 82 with ten. Numbers clearly matter: each firm's mark-up satisfies (P − MC)/P = sᵢ/|ε|, so concentration translates directly into market power, which is why competition authorities track the HHI.

Yet Bertrand competition with identical goods gives P = MC = 30 with only two firms, far better for consumers than Cournot with ten. Stackelberg, where one firm commits to its output first, gives Q = 67.5 and P = 52.5, more competitive than simultaneous Cournot with the same two firms. For a given n, the timing and the choice of strategic variable change prices a great deal, which supports the claim.

However, the mode of competition is not arbitrary. Kreps and Scheinkman (1983) show that when firms first choose capacity and then compete on price, the outcome matches Cournot. Product differentiation also gives Bertrand firms market power. In many industries, then, Cournot is the better reduced form, and in Cournot numbers matter.

Collusion strengthens the role of numbers. In repeated play, any of these structures can sustain prices near monopoly if firms are patient. With equal shares, the gain from cheating rises relative to each firm's collusive profit as n grows, so collusion becomes harder in less concentrated markets. Here the number of firms affects consumers through the sustainability of collusion as well as through static competition.

The claim is therefore overstated. How firms compete matters greatly for a given structure, but it depends partly on capacity and products that are themselves shaped by structure, and the number of firms affects both static mark-ups and the risk of coordination. Good policy, for example merger control assessing both unilateral and coordinated effects, needs to consider both.

questions.q: "A Pigouvian tax is always the best way to deal with a negative externality." Critically evaluate this proposition, comparing Pigouvian taxes with Coasean bargaining, quantity regulation and tradable permits. Refer to carbon emissions where helpful.
markScheme: Explains the externality: marginal social cost exceeds marginal private cost, so the market overproduces with a DWL
Pigouvian tax equal to marginal external damage at the efficient output restores efficiency (Pigou, 1920)
Advantages: equalises marginal abatement costs across firms (cost-effectiveness), provides a dynamic incentive to innovate, raises revenue
Information problem: the planner must know marginal damage at the optimum; damage is hard to value (e.g. the social cost of carbon)
Coase (1960): with clear rights and low transaction costs bargaining is efficient; it fails with many parties, free-riding and asymmetric information
Command-and-control standards are simple and certain but not cost-effective when abatement costs differ
Tradable permits fix quantity and let price adjust; with full information and no uncertainty they equal a tax
Weitzman (1974): under cost uncertainty, prefer prices when marginal damage is flat relative to marginal abatement cost, quantities when it is steep
Carbon: damage depends on the stock, so the marginal damage of a year's flow is fairly flat, which favours prices in the short run; hybrid schemes such as a cap with a price floor are common
Other issues: distribution and regressivity, leakage and border adjustment, political economy, interaction with existing distortions
Reasoned conclusion: taxes are often the best single tool, but not always; the best choice depends on information, uncertainty, transaction costs and politics
questions.modelAnswer:
A negative externality makes marginal social cost exceed marginal private cost, so a competitive market produces too much and creates a deadweight loss. Pigou (1920) proposed a tax equal to marginal external damage at the efficient output. Firms then internalise the harm and choose the efficient quantity.

The tax has strong advantages. Every firm abates until its marginal abatement cost equals the tax, so a given reduction is achieved at least total cost, without the regulator knowing individual costs. It rewards every unit cut, which gives a continuing incentive to innovate, and it raises revenue that can reduce other distorting taxes.

But "always" is too strong. The tax must be set at marginal damage at the optimum, which requires knowledge regulators often lack. For carbon, estimates of the social cost depend heavily on discounting and assumptions about climate damage.

Coase (1960) showed that with clear property rights and low transaction costs, bargaining achieves efficiency without government pricing. A tax on top of a Coasean bargain could even overcorrect. Bargaining fails, however, with many dispersed parties, free-riding and private information, which is exactly the case for carbon.

Command-and-control standards give certainty and are easy to monitor but are not cost-effective when abatement costs differ, and they offer no reward for going beyond the standard. Tradable permits fix the quantity and let the market set the price. With full information they match a tax. Under uncertainty about abatement costs, Weitzman (1974) showed that a price instrument is better when marginal damage is flat relative to marginal abatement cost, and a quantity instrument when damage rises steeply. Because climate damage depends on the stock of CO₂, one year's emissions have a fairly flat marginal damage, which favours prices in the short run. Thresholds may favour caps over longer horizons.

In practice hybrids are common. The UK ETS caps emissions but sets an auction reserve price, which puts a floor under the permit price. Distributional effects, carbon leakage and political acceptability also matter. A Pigouvian tax is often the best single instrument, but whether it is best depends on information, uncertainty and institutions.
